Huntington divided the world into the following major civilizations:[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-34)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:1-3)

*   [Western civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world") (or colloquially as _[Christendom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christendom "Christendom")_), comprising the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe") and [Central Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Europe "Central Europe"), most of the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), and [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania "Oceania"). Whether Latin America and the [former member states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Soviet_states "Post-Soviet states") of the Soviet Union are included, or are instead their own separate civilizations, will be an important future consideration for those regions, according to Huntington. The traditional Western viewpoint identified Western Civilization with the [Western Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Christianity "Western Christianity") ([Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church")-[Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism")) countries and culture. 
    *   [Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") civilization, including [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") (excluding [Guyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyana "Guyana"), [Suriname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suriname "Suriname") and [French Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Guiana "French Guiana")), [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), and the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic") may be considered a part of Western civilization. Many people in [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America"), [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") and [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") regard themselves as full members of Western civilization.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The [Southern Cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Cone "Southern Cone") is, demographically speaking, the most Western region in Latin America.
    *   [Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") civilization, comprising [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria"), [Cyprus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus "Cyprus"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country) "Georgia (country)"), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"), [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania"), great parts of the former [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Soviet_states "Post-Soviet states") and [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"). 
        *   Countries with a non-Orthodox majority are usually excluded e.g. Muslim [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan") and Muslim [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania "Albania") and most of [Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia"), as well as majority Muslim regions in the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"), [Caucasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasus "Caucasus") and central [Russian regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_subjects_of_Russia "Federal subjects of Russia") such as [Tatarstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatarstan "Tatarstan") and [Bashkortostan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bashkortostan "Bashkortostan"), Roman Catholic [Slovenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenia "Slovenia") and [Croatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia "Croatia"), Protestant and Catholic [Baltic states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_states "Baltic states"). However, [Armenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenia "Armenia") is included, despite its dominant faith, the [Armenian Apostolic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Apostolic_Church "Armenian Apostolic Church"), being a part of [Oriental Orthodoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriental_Orthodoxy "Oriental Orthodoxy") rather than the [Eastern Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church"). [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan") is also included, despite its dominant faith being [Sunni Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunni_Islam "Sunni Islam"), though this is likely due to there being an Orthodox plurality at the time of publication.

*   The [Eastern world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") is the mix of the [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic "Islamic"), [Sinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_China "Greater China"), [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism "Hinduism")-[Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") ([Dharmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_religions "Indian religions") and [Indic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_India "Greater India")), and [Japonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") civilizations. 
    *   The [Sinic civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asian_cultural_sphere "East Asian cultural sphere") of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), the [Koreas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"), [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), and [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam"). This group also includes the [Chinese diaspora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overseas_Chinese "Overseas Chinese"), especially in relation to Southeast Asia.
    *   [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), considered a hybrid of [Chinese civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_culture "Chinese culture") and older [Altaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altaic_languages "Altaic languages") patterns.
    *   The [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") cultures of [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka"), [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"), [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodia "Cambodia"); and also [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"), [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia"), and [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan"), are identified as separate from other civilizations, but Huntington believes that they do not constitute a major civilization in the sense of international affairs.
    *   The [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism "Hinduism") civilization (or colloquially as _[Hindudom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindudom "Hindudom")_), located chiefly in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") and [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"), and culturally adhered to by the global [Indian diaspora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-resident_Indian_and_person_of_Indian_origin "Non-resident Indian and person of Indian origin").
    *   Part of [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic "Islamic"), located in Islamic countries which includes [South Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") countries of [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") and [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"); and [South East Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") countries of [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") and [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia").

*   The [Muslim world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_world "Muslim world") of the [Greater Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Middle_East "Greater Middle East") (excluding [Armenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenia "Armenia"), [Cyprus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus "Cyprus"), [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country) "Georgia (country)"), [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"), [Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malta "Malta") and [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan")), northern [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa"), [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania "Albania"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"), parts of [Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Bosnia and Herzegovina"), [Brunei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunei "Brunei"), [Comoros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comoros "Comoros"), [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Maldives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maldives "Maldives") and parts of south-western Philippines.
*   The civilization of [Sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") located in southern Africa, Middle Africa (excluding Chad), East Africa (excluding [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"), the [Comoros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comoros "Comoros"), [Mauritius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritius "Mauritius"), and the [Swahili coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_coast "Swahili coast") of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") and [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania")), [Cape Verde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verde "Cape Verde"), [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana"), the [Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast"), [Liberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberia "Liberia"), and [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone"). Considered as a possible eighth civilization by Huntington.
*   [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") is a stand-alone nation once part of the Western world, now belonging to the African world. [Afrikaners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaners "Afrikaners") and [White South Africans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_South_Africans "White South Africans") are part of the Western world, while [Black South Africans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_South_Africa "Ethnic groups in South Africa") are the majority and dominate South African politics. The latter do not identify as Westerners, instead affiliating themselves with Africans. South Africa is also a [Civilization state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization_state "Civilization state") because it aims to represent the whole of the African world, including the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). [Pan-Africanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Africanism "Pan-Africanism") is the leading ideology in South Africa; it opposes the west in the international stage.
*   Instead of belonging to one of the major civilizations, [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia") and [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti") are labeled as _Lone_ countries. [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") could be considered a unique state with its own civilization, Huntington writes, but one which is extremely similar to the West. Huntington also believes that the [Anglophone Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Caribbean "Commonwealth Caribbean"), former [British colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_colonies "British colonies") in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"), constitutes a distinct entity.
*   There are also others which are considered cleft countries because they contain very large groups of people identifying with separate civilizations. Examples include [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") (cleft between its [Eastern Rite Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Greek_Catholic_Church "Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church")-dominated [western section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Ukraine "Western Ukraine") and its [Moscow Patriarchate Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Orthodox_Church_(Moscow_Patriarchate) "Ukrainian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate)")-dominated [eastern section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Ukraine "Eastern Ukraine")), [French Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Guiana "French Guiana") (cleft between Latin America, and the West), [Benin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin "Benin"), [Chad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad "Chad"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria"), [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), and [Togo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Togo "Togo") (all cleft between Islam and Sub-Saharan Africa), [Guyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyana "Guyana") and [Suriname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suriname "Suriname") (cleft between Hindu and Sub-Saharan African), [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka") and [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan") (cleft between Hindu and Buddhist, although it can be put under the larger [Dharmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_religions "Indian religions") civilisation), and the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") (cleft between Islam, in the case of south western [Mindanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao "Mindanao"); Sinic, in the case of [Cordillera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Administrative_Region "Cordillera Administrative Region"); and the westernized Christian-majority). [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan") was also included as cleft between Islam and Sub-Saharan Africa; this division became a formal split in July 2011 following an overwhelming vote for independence by [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan") in a [January 2011 referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudanese_independence_referendum,_2011 "South Sudanese independence referendum, 2011").

### Civilizational clash

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Civilizational clash")]

[![Image 7: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. [![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Samuel_P._Huntington_%282004_World_Economic_Forum%29.jpg/250px-Samuel_P._Huntington_%282004_World_Economic_Forum%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_P._Huntington_(2004_World_Economic_Forum).jpg)

Huntington at the 2004 [World Economic Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Economic_Forum "World Economic Forum")

Huntington argues that the trends of global conflict after the end of the Cold War are increasingly appearing at these civilizational divisions. Wars such as those following the break up of [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"), in [Chechnya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechnya "Chechnya"), and [between India and Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_wars_and_conflicts "Indo-Pakistani wars and conflicts") were cited as evidence of inter-civilizational conflict. He also argues that the widespread Western belief in the universality of the West's values and political systems is naïve and that continued insistence on democratization and such universal norms will only further antagonize other civilizations. Huntington sees the West as reluctant to accept this because it built the international system, wrote its laws, and gave it substance in the form of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

Huntington identifies a major shift of economic, military, and political power from the West to the other civilizations of the world, most significantly to what he identifies as the two challenger civilizations, Sinic and Islam.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

In Huntington's view, East Asian Sinic civilization is culturally asserting itself and its values relative to the West due to its rapid economic growth. Specifically, he believes that China's goals are to reassert itself as the regional [hegemon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegemon "Hegemon"), and that other countries in the region will bandwagon with China due to the history of hierarchical command structures implicit in the [Confucian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucian "Confucian") Sinic civilization, as opposed to the individualism and pluralism valued in the West. Regional powers such as the two Koreas and Vietnam will acquiesce to Chinese demands and become more supportive of China rather than attempting to oppose it. Huntington therefore believes that the rise of China poses one of the most significant problems and the most powerful long-term threat to the West, as Chinese cultural assertion clashes with the American desire for the lack of a regional hegemony in East Asia.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-35)

Huntington argues that the Islamic civilization has experienced a massive population explosion which is fueling instability both on the [borders of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisions_of_the_world_in_Islam "Divisions of the world in Islam") and in its interior, where [fundamentalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_fundamentalism "Islamic fundamentalism") movements are becoming increasingly popular. Manifestations of what he terms the [Islamic resurgence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_revival "Islamic revival") include the [1979 Iranian revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Iranian_revolution "1979 Iranian revolution") and the first [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War"). Perhaps the most controversial statement Huntington made in the _Foreign Affairs_ article was, "Islam has bloody borders". Huntington believes this to be a real consequence of several factors, including the previously mentioned Muslim [youth bulge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_pyramid "Population pyramid") and population growth and Islamic proximity to many civilizations including Sinic, Orthodox, Western, and African.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

Huntington sees Islamic civilization as a potential ally to China, both having more revisionist goals and sharing common conflicts with other civilizations, especially the West. Specifically, he identifies common Chinese and Islamic interests in the areas of weapons proliferation, human rights, and democracy that conflict with those of the West, and feels that these are areas in which the two civilizations will cooperate.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

Russia, Japan, and India are what Huntington terms swing civilizations and may favor either side. Russia, for example, clashes with the many Muslim ethnic groups on its southern border (such as [Chechnya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechnya "Chechnya")) but—according to Huntington—cooperates with Iran to avoid further Muslim-Orthodox violence in Southern Russia, and to help continue the flow of oil. Huntington argues that a [Sino-Islamic connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Islamic_connection?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sino-Islamic connection (page does not exist)") is emerging in which China will cooperate more closely with [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), and other states to augment its international position.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

Huntington also argues that civilizational conflicts are particularly prevalent between Muslims and non-Muslims, identifying the bloody borders between [Islamic and non-Islamic civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisions_of_the_world_in_Islam "Divisions of the world in Islam"). This conflict dates back as far as the [initial thrust of Islam into Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_conquest_of_Hispania "Umayyad conquest of Hispania"), its eventual expulsion in the [Iberian reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista"), the attacks of the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Turks "Ottoman Turks") on [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe") and [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), and the European imperial division of the Islamic nations in the 1800s and 1900s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

Huntington also believes that some of the factors contributing to this conflict are that both Christianity (upon which Western civilization is based) and Islam are:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

*   Missionary religions, seeking conversion of others
*   Universal, all-or-nothing religions, in the sense that it is believed by both sides that only their faith is the correct one
*   [Teleological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleological "Teleological") religions, that is, that their values and beliefs represent the goals of existence and purpose in human existence.

More recent factors contributing to a Western–Islamic clash, Huntington wrote, are the [Islamic Resurgence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_revival "Islamic revival") and demographic explosion in Islam, coupled with the values of Western universalism—that is, the view that all civilizations should adopt Western values—that infuriate Islamic fundamentalists. All these historical and modern factors combined, Huntington wrote briefly in his _Foreign Affairs_ article and in much more detail in his 1996 book, would lead to a bloody clash between the Islamic and Western civilizations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

#### _Causes_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Causes")]

Huntington offers six explanations for why he thinks civilizations will clash:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

1.   Differences among civilizations are too basic in that civilizations are differentiated from each other by history, language, culture, tradition, and, most importantly, religion. These fundamental differences are the product of centuries and the foundations of different civilizations, meaning they will not be gone soon.
2.   The world is becoming a smaller place. As a result, interactions across the world are increasing, which intensify civilization consciousness and the awareness of differences between civilizations and commonalities within civilizations.
3.   Due to economic modernization and social change, people are separated from longstanding local identities. Instead, religion has replaced this gap, which provides a basis for identity and commitment that transcends national boundaries and unites civilizations.
4.   The growth of civilization-consciousness is enhanced by the dual role of the West. On the one hand, the West is at a peak of power. At the same time, a return-to-the-roots phenomenon is occurring among non-Western civilizations. A West at the peak of its power confronts non-Western countries that increasingly have the desire, the will and the resources to shape the world in non-Western ways.
5.   Cultural characteristics and differences are less mutable and hence less easily compromised and resolved than political and economic ones.
6.   Economic regionalism is increasing. Successful economic regionalism will reinforce civilization-consciousness. Economic regionalism may succeed only when it is rooted in a common civilization.

#### _The West versus 'the Rest'_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: The West versus 'the Rest'")]

Huntington suggests that in the future the central axis of world politics tends to be the conflict between Western and non-Western civilizations, in [Stuart Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Hall_(cultural_theorist) "Stuart Hall (cultural theorist)")'s phrase, the conflict between the West and 'the Rest'. He offers three forms of general and fundamental actions that non-Western civilization can take in response to Western countries.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-36)

1.   Non-Western countries can attempt to achieve isolation in order to preserve their own values and protect themselves from Western invasion. However, Huntington argues that the costs of this action are high and only a few states can pursue it.
2.   According to the theory of [bandwagoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandwagoning "Bandwagoning"), non-Western countries can join and accept Western values.
3.   Non-Western countries can make an effort to balance Western power through modernization. They can develop economic/military power and cooperate with other non-Western countries against the West while still preserving their own values and institutions. Huntington believes that the increasing power of non-Western civilizations in international society will make the West begin to develop a better understanding of the cultural fundamentals underlying other civilizations. Therefore, Western civilization will cease to be regarded as universal but different civilizations will learn to coexist and join to shape the future world.

#### _Core state and fault line conflicts_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Core state and fault line conflicts")]

In Huntington's view, intercivilizational conflict manifests itself in two forms: fault line conflicts and core state conflicts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

_[Fault line conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault\_line\_war "Fault line war")_ are on a local level and occur between adjacent states belonging to different civilizations or within states that are home to populations from different civilizations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:0-2)

_Core state conflicts_ are on a global level between the major states of different civilizations. Core state conflicts can arise out of fault line conflicts when core states become involved.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-Huntington1-37)

These conflicts may result from a number of causes, such as: relative influence or power (military or economic), discrimination against people from a different civilization, intervention to protect kinsmen in a different civilization, or different values and culture, particularly when one civilization attempts to impose its values on people of a different civilization.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-Huntington1-37)

#### Modernization, Westernization, and _torn_ countries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Modernization, Westernization, and torn countries")]

[Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") and the [Four Asian Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Asian_Tigers "Four Asian Tigers") have modernized in many respects while maintaining traditional or authoritarian societies which distinguish them from the West. Some of these countries have clashed with the West and some have not.

Perhaps the ultimate example of non-Western modernization is Russia, the core state of the [Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodoxy "Eastern Orthodoxy") civilization. Huntington argues that Russia is primarily a non-Western state although he seems to agree that it shares a considerable amount of cultural ancestry with the modern West. According to Huntington, the West is distinguished from Orthodox Christian countries by its experience of the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance"), [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation"), the [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment"); by overseas [colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism") rather than contiguous expansion and colonialism; and by the infusion of [Classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity") culture through [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") rather than through the continuous trajectory of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire").

Huntington refers to countries that are seeking to affiliate with another civilization as torn countries. [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), whose political leadership has systematically tried to Westernize the country since the 1920s, is his chief example. Turkey's history, culture, and traditions are derived from Islamic civilization, but Turkey's elite, beginning with [Mustafa Kemal Atatürk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustafa_Kemal_Atat%C3%BCrk "Mustafa Kemal Atatürk") who took power as [first President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Turkey "President of Turkey") in 1923, imposed Western institutions and dress, embraced the [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet"), joined [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO"), and has sought to [join the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union%E2%80%93Turkey_relations "European Union–Turkey relations").

Mexico and Russia are also considered to be torn by Huntington. He also gives the example of Australia as a country torn between its Western civilizational heritage and its growing economic engagement with Asia.

According to Huntington, a torn country must meet three requirements to redefine its civilizational identity. Its political and economic elite must support the move. Second, the public must be willing to accept the redefinition. Third, the elites of the civilization that the torn country is trying to join must accept the country.

The book claims that to date no torn country has successfully redefined its civilizational identity, this mostly due to the elites of the host civilization refusing to accept the torn country, though if Turkey gained membership in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), it has been noted that many of its people would support Westernization, as in the following quote by EU Minister [Egemen Bağış](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egemen_Ba%C4%9F%C4%B1%C5%9F "Egemen Bağış"): "This is what Europe needs to do: they need to say that when Turkey fulfills all requirements, Turkey will become a member of the EU on date X. Then, we will regain the Turkish public opinion support in one day."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-38) If this were to happen, it would, according to Huntington, be the first to redefine its civilizational identity.

## Influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Influence")]

The clash of civilizations theory made a substantial scholarly and policy impact.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:4-11) It has been widely cited, both in academic studies, and by various political figures, with studies documenting specific influences of the clash of civilizations theory. The [war on terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror") has been theorized as both an accurate prediction of the theory, and as a result of both Western and Islamist leaders adopting the premise of a clash between their cultures.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:5-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:6-13) The theory has been described as a paradigm that is particularly prevalent in [right wing politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_wing_politics "Right wing politics") across Western democracies, and was viewed as part of the [Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_2016_presidential_campaign "Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:7-15) The theory has been used to describe [right-wing ideology in Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right_politics_in_Israel "Far-right politics in Israel"), particularly to justify clashes between [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews_in_Israel "Jews in Israel") and [Palestinians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinians "Palestinians").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-39) It had been observed as influencing the worldview of Israeli Prime Minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu") on Islam.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:8-16) The clash of civilizations had also influenced [Viktor Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Orb%C3%A1n "Viktor Orbán") in his rejection of [multi-culturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-culturalism "Multi-culturalism") and in adding restrictions for Muslim immigration.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:9-17)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Criticism")]

The book has been criticized by various academic writers, who have empirically, historically, logically, or ideologically challenged its claims.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-43) Political scientist [Paul Musgrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Musgrave "Paul Musgrave") writes that _Clash of Civilization_ "enjoys great cachet among the sort of policymaker who enjoys name-dropping [Sun Tzu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Tzu "Sun Tzu"), but few specialists in international relations rely on it or even cite it approvingly. Bluntly, _Clash_ has not proven to be a useful or accurate guide to understanding the world."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:13-22) Other books, written for the general public, similarly challenge Huntington's contentious claims. For example, in his work _Identity and Violence: The Illusion of Destiny_, The Nobel laureate [Amartya Sen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amartya_Sen "Amartya Sen") advances several critiques of Huntington's main concept of an inevitable _Clash_ along civilizational lines. He argues that violence occurs when individuals see each other as having a singular affiliation (e.g., [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindus "Hindus"), [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims"), [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians")), as opposed to multiple affiliations: e.g., Hindu, woman, housewife, mother, artist, daughter, member of a particular socio-economic class etc. In this sense, and to the detriment of civilization distinctiveness, it is argued that all of these dimensions can, and should be a source of a personal identity.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-44)

Moreover, in an article explicitly referring to Huntington, the same scholar [Amartya Sen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amartya_Sen "Amartya Sen") (1999) argues that "diversity is a feature of most cultures in the world. Western civilization is no exception. The practice of democracy that has won out in the modern West is largely a result of a consensus that has emerged since the [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") and the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), and particularly in the last century or so. To read in this a historical commitment of the West—over the millennia—to democracy, and then to contrast it with non-Western traditions (treating each as monolithic) would be a great mistake."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:10-18):16

In his 2003 book _[Terror and Liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terror\_and\_Liberalism "Terror and Liberalism")_, [Paul Berman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Berman "Paul Berman") argues that distinct cultural boundaries do not exist in the present day. He argues there is "no Islamic civilization nor a Western civilization", and that the evidence for a civilization clash is not convincing, especially when considering relationships such as that between the [United States and Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia%E2%80%93United_States_relations "Saudi Arabia–United States relations"). In addition, he cites the fact that many Islamic extremists spent a significant amount of time living or studying in the Western world. According to Berman, conflict arises because of [philosophical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") beliefs various groups share (or do not share), regardless of cultural or religious identity.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:14-23)

[Timothy Garton Ash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Garton_Ash "Timothy Garton Ash") objects to the "extreme cultural determinism... crude to the point of parody" of Huntington's idea that Catholic and Protestant Europe is headed for democracy, but that Orthodox Christian and Islamic Europe must accept dictatorship.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:12-20)

In November 2001, [Noam Chomsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noam_Chomsky "Noam Chomsky") said the concept of the clash of civilizations was merely a pretext to continue the same aggressive foreign policy as during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), only with new antagonists in place of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:17-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-46) He said that the concept has allowed the US to ignore its support for "[Islamic fundamentalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_fundamentalism "Islamic fundamentalism")" Saudi Arabia.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:17-45)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:3-47)

[Nathan J. Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_J._Robinson "Nathan J. Robinson") criticizes Huntington's thesis as inconsistent. He notes that according to Huntington, "[Spanish-speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanophone "Hispanophone") Catholic-majority [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") is West, while Spanish-speaking Catholic-majority [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") is not part of Western civilization, and instead belongs with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") as part of [Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") civilization." Robinson concludes, "If you look at the map and think these divisions make sense, which you might, it is because what you are mostly seeing here is a map of prejudices. [Huntington] indeed shows how a lot of people think of the world, especially in America."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:3-47)

The literary criticism podcast _[If Books Could Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If\_Books\_Could\_Kill "If Books Could Kill")_ raises the concern that Huntington may be seen as publishing [genocide apologia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_justification "Genocide justification"), uncritically repeating verbatim the assertions of [Serbian soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_Armed_Forces "Serbian Armed Forces") during the [Bosnian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_genocide "Bosnian genocide") that ethnic cleansing is necessary due to the high Muslim Albanian [birth rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_rate "Birth rate").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-48)

### Opposing concepts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Opposing concepts")]

The clash of civilizations has been criticized as promoting an ideologically [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism") attempt to maintain the [imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism") gains from [Western colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_colonialism "Western colonialism").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-49)[Edward Said](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Said "Edward Said") issued a response to Huntington's thesis in his 2001 article, _The Clash of Ignorance_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:11-19) Said argues that Huntington's categorization of the world's fixed civilizations "omits the dynamic interdependency and interaction of culture". A longtime critic of the Huntingtonian paradigm, and an outspoken proponent of Arab issues, Said (2004) also argues that the clash of civilizations thesis is an example of "the purest invidious racism, a sort of parody of Hitlerian science directed today against Arabs and Muslims" (p.293).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-50)

_[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_ columnist [Janan Ganesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janan_Ganesh "Janan Ganesh") argued in 2025 that Huntington's theory had fared poorly on recent evidence, as the most significant conflicts have occurred within and not between Huntington's civilizational groupings. Whereas Huntington had predicted conflict to occur between 'civilizations' at the borders between them, the most protracted and deadly wars – Ganesh highlighted the [Russo-Ukrainian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022%E2%80%93present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)"), the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"), the [Sudanese civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_civil_war_(2023%E2%80%93present) "Sudanese civil war (2023–present)") and the [Yemeni civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_civil_war_(2014%E2%80%93present) "Yemeni civil war (2014–present)") – have occurred between groups belonging to similar cultures and religions. Similarly, where Huntington said that Islam had "bloody borders", most of the victims of [Islamic extremism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_extremism "Islamic extremism") have been Muslims. Ganesh noted the reliability of cross-civilizational partnerships between [Russia and China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Russia_relations "China–Russia relations") and between Japan and Europe, which he said stand in contrast to bitter intra-civilizational rivalries such as the [Iran–Saudi Arabia proxy war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_proxy_war "Iran–Saudi Arabia proxy war") and the potential for conflict between [China and Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-strait_relations "Cross-strait relations"). It is "the doubter, the apostate and the schismatic" who receive the most hostility, Ganesh wrote. He suggested that a similar logic explained the [Trump administration's preference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_second_Trump_administration "Foreign policy of the second Trump administration") for countries such as Russia and Saudi Arabia over culturally closer nations in Europe. Ganesh stated that the [Israel–Palestine conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict") is notable for being an exception that fits Huntington's model. He concluded that the often overlooked [2008 Russo-Georgian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Georgian_War "Russo-Georgian War") was a stronger symbolic inauguration of the current era than the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:02-21)

In _[21 Lessons for the 21st Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21\_Lessons\_for\_the\_21st\_Century "21 Lessons for the 21st Century")_, [Yuval Noah Harari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuval_Noah_Harari "Yuval Noah Harari") called the clash of civilizations a misleading thesis. He wrote that [Islamic fundamentalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_fundamentalism "Islamic fundamentalism") is more of a threat to a [global civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_civilization "Planetary civilization"), rather than a confrontation with the West. He also argued that talking about civilizations using analogies from evolutionary biology is wrong.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:15-24)

In his 1993 article, Huntington wrote that "If civilization is what counts … the likelihood of violence between Ukrainians and Russians should be low. They are two Slavic, primarily Orthodox peoples who have had close relationships with each other for centuries". In 2022, Russia [invaded Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine"), having [annexed Crimea in 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Russian_annexation_of_Crimea "2014 Russian annexation of Crimea") and then [supported separatists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_separatist_forces_in_Ukraine "Russian separatist forces in Ukraine") in the [War in Donbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Donbas "War in Donbas")[(2014–2022)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Donbas "War in Donbas").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-:16-25)

#### Intermediate Region

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Intermediate Region")]

Huntington's geopolitical model, especially the structures for [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa") and [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasia "Eurasia"), is largely derived from the [Intermediate Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_Region "Intermediate Region") geopolitical model first formulated by [Dimitri Kitsikis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitri_Kitsikis "Dimitri Kitsikis") and published in 1978.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-51) The Intermediate Region, which spans the [Adriatic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") and the [Indus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_River "Indus River"), is neither Western nor Eastern (at least, with respect to the [Far East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_East "Far East")) but is considered distinct. Concerning this region, Huntington departs from Kitsikis contending that a civilizational fault line exists between the two dominant yet differing religions ([Eastern Orthodoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") and [Sunni Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunni_Islam "Sunni Islam")), hence a dynamic of external conflict. However, Kitsikis establishes an integrated civilization comprising these two peoples along with those belonging to the less dominant religions of [Shia Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shia_Islam "Shia Islam"), [Alevism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alevism "Alevism"), and [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism"). They have a set of mutual cultural, social, economic and political views and norms which radically differ from those in the West and the Far East. In the Intermediate Region, therefore, one cannot speak of a civilizational clash or external conflict, but rather an internal conflict, not for cultural domination, but for political succession. This has been successfully demonstrated by documenting the [rise of Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Christianity "History of Christianity") from the [Hellenized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenization "Hellenization")[Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), the rise of the [Islamic caliphates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate "Caliphate") from the [Christianized Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") and the rise of [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") from the Islamic caliphates and the Christianized Roman Empire.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Dialogue Among Civilizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clash_of_Civilizations&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Dialogue Among Civilizations")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/World_Economic_Forum_Annual_Meeting_Davos_2007.jpg/250px-World_Economic_Forum_Annual_Meeting_Davos_2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Economic_Forum_Annual_Meeting_Davos_2007.jpg)

[Mohammad Khatami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Khatami "Mohammad Khatami"), [reformist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Reformists "Iranian Reformists") president of [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") (in office 1997–2005), introduced the theory of _Dialogue Among Civilizations_ as a response to Huntington's theory.

In recent years, the theory of _[Dialogue Among Civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialogue\_Among\_Civilizations "Dialogue Among Civilizations")_, a response to Huntington's _Clash of Civilizations_, has become the center of some international attention. The concept was originally coined by Austrian philosopher [Hans Köchler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_K%C3%B6chler "Hans Köchler") in an essay on cultural identity (1972).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-52) In a letter to [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO"), Köchler had earlier proposed that the cultural organization of the United Nations should take up the issue of a "dialogue between different civilizations" (_dialogue entre les différentes civilisations_).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-53) In 2001, [Mohammad Khatami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Khatami "Mohammad Khatami"), then [Iranian president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_president "Iranian president"), introduced the concept at the global level. At his initiative, the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") proclaimed the year 2001 as the "United Nations Year of Dialogue among Civilizations".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_of_Civilizations#cite_note-56)

The [Alliance of Civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Civilizations "Alliance of Civilizations") (AOC) initiative was proposed at the 59th [General Assembly of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") in 2005 by the [Spanish Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Spain "Prime Minister of Spain"), [José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Luis_Rodr%C3%ADguez_Zapatero "José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero") and co-sponsored by the [Turkish Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Turkey "Prime Minister of Turkey")[Recep Tayyip Erdoğan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan "Recep Tayyip Erdoğan"). The initiative is intended to galvanize collective action across diverse societies to combat [extremism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremism "Extremism"), to overcome cultural and social barriers between mainly the [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world") and predominantly [Muslim worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world "Islamic world"), and to reduce the tensions and polarization between societies which differ in religious and cultural values.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 23: 2026 is a special year for Colorado, as we celebrate our 150th anniversary in the same year that the United States celebrates the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence - the only state to do so! “ ( To celebrate, the America 250 - Colorado 150 Commission invites all Coloradans to acknowledge our complete shared history, honor what makes Colorado unique, and recognize our shared destiny as we strive toward a more perfect union. Oops 😅 While Cape Town is pretty special, don’t worry, there are other [@silentbookclub](https://www.instagram.com/silentbookclub/) chapters across the country (even if they aren’t reading in the street... yet)! 🚧  
  
🗺️ According to the Silent Book Club website map, there are now 26 chapters in South Africa alone (and 5 more in other Southern African countries).   
  
There are chapters in the Western Cape, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KZN, Eastern Cape, and Free State! And in Zimbabwe, Zambia, and Botswana. 🇿🇦🇿🇼🇿🇲🇧🇼  
  
So if you can’t join the Cape Town chapter, you should definitely join your local chapter! And if you don’t have a chapter, maybe you should start one 🙌

# [Song for Nagasaki / Bells of Nagasaki](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2026/8/22/song-of-nagasaki-bells-of-nagasaki)

Are you the type of reader that likes someone else’s summary? Then pick up [A Song for Nagasaki](https://a.co/d/0glqFGPQ). Or, alternatively, [The Bells of Nagasaki](https://a.co/d/05Smsd3U) is the book for those of you who prefer to go straight to the source. Either way, you are in for a powerful read.

Both books tell the story of Dr. Takashi Nagai. Dr. Nagai became a Catholic after serving as a doctor for the Japanese army in their invasion of China, in the 1930s. He was part of the thriving Catholic community of Nagasaki, Japan - a community which had survived many waves of intense persecution over the centuries, and numbered 12,000 strong. The Nagasaki Cathedral was the largest church building in Asia, at the time.

On August 9, 1945, Dr. Nagai was at work as the dean of the medical school in the Urakami neighborhood, north of the main city which wrapped around a fjord-like harbor. His specialty was the new field of X-rays, and he had just been diagnosed with leukemia from exposure during experimentation and implementation of the new technology.

The, at 11:02 am, the second atomic bomb dropped by the United States exploded 500 meters above the nearby Cathedral and the pressure wave ripped through the building he was in.

Both books tell what happened next, and how Dr. Nagai responded. The story is fascinating and shocking. If you want to know more, buy one or both of the books … or come to the CTR retreat on October 3!

# [Impact Networks](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2026/5/24/impact-networks)

[![Image 5](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/fc05915f-5086-4974-81e9-1ae7113dac3d/Impact+Networks.jpg)](https://www.amazon.com/Impact-Networks-Connection-Collaboration-Catalyze/dp/1523091681/ref=tmm_pap_swatch_0)

_Review by Thomas Cogdell_

I read [Impact Networks](https://www.amazon.com/Impact-Networks-Connection-Collaboration-Catalyze/dp/1523091681/ref=tmm_pap_swatch_0) by David Erlichman on the plane flying from Austin to Los Angeles. Usually I’m skeptical of business-y type books … as Dilbert is fond of pointing out, there are 500+ published every year, each one of them promising that _theirs_ is the key to success! To try to read, process, and put into practice even one of them - not to mention all 500! - would be exhausting and chaotic.

But … this book was recommended by a trusted friend Shane Stephens. So I bought a copy and figured a plane trip was a good time to see if it was worthwhile.

Little did I know I would end up weeping in seat 17A! This book didn’t tell me _what_ to do in the future … it explained why what I was already doing was working even though it always proved hard to explain.

For example: Antioch Network. I am privileged to serve on the leadership council of AN. It’s been a running joke for over a decade that nobody can quite describe what AN does or how it works. We just follow a few principles the Lord has given us (like, “Do nothing to grow Antioch Network”) and watch the Holy Spirit work in mighty ways. The typical business / non-profit model doesn’t fit for us.

Impact Networks explains in coherent language why that is. The book begins by saying that the problems that the world is facing are increasingly complex and even chaotic. Traditional organizational structures - hierarchical, top-down, controlled - are very good at addressing simple problems. But they fail when it comes to complex problems.

Instead, a new form of structure is proving successful at addressing complex / chaotic problems. They call these structures “Impact Networks" - thus the title of the book. (The subtitle is also worth noting: “Create Connection, Spark Collaboration, and Catalyze Systemic Change”).

One aspect of this structure is that the focus is not on the organization, but the mission. This diagram from page 41 shows this difference:

![Image 6](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/ce47861a-3c04-49cb-b2cd-5ea89bc3c8f4/Impact+Networks+-+diagram.jpg)

Erlichman writes in this context that “While hierarchical leaders focus on the quantity and quality of _their_ own relationships with others, network leaders focus on increasing the quantity and quality of relationships _between_ others.” This sounds a lot like working for unity in the body of Christ!

Though not written from an explicitly Christian standpoint, there is much in the book that applies to our mission at Christ the Reconciler. We are in contact with multiple networks that fit this book’s description of impact networks, including Antioch Network, Dream Together 2030, and NAN / IPECC. We flow fluidly in and out of active engagement with these networks as needed.

Throughout, our overriding focus is not “utility” (what can these networks do for us) but relationship - how to deepen and prioritize our relationships. I will close with this beautiful passage from the book, that explains the wisdom of this approach:

Impact networks are only as strong as the relationships that hold them together. Relationships influence nearly everything a network aims to achieve, including how information is shared, how decisions are made, and how work gets done. When relationships deepen to a point of mutual confidence, where two people feel they can count on each other to act in service to the purpose - even if they might disagree - we call that trust … I mean trust for impact. This is the type of trusting relationship that allows people to hold the tension through disagreement and conflict, find common ground, and work together to achieve mutual goals … we have consistently found that trust is the single most important factor behind successful impact networks: _networks move at the speed of trust._

# [Jacob Deshazar: Forgive Your Enemies](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2025/12/27/jacob-deshazar-forgive-your-enemies)

[![Image 7](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/d3534b63-b9df-46ac-b6b6-bc5383961a40/Jacob+Deshazar.jpg)](https://a.co/d/8xbvFcc)

[Jacob Deshazar: Forgive Your Enemies](https://a.co/d/8xbvFcc) is in a children’s series of books on Christian Heroes. It tells the story of one of Doolittle’s Raiders, who conducted the first US bombing run on the Japanese islands in 1942. All of the planes ran out of gas over occupied China after conducting the mission, and one of the airmen who was captured by the Japanese was … Jacob Deshazar.

Jacob was filled with anger towards the Japanese during most of his captivity - for their cruelty, the execution of some of his compatriots, and their lack of adherence with UN rules for treating POWs. I won’t ruin the story of how his attitude was turned around, but suffice it to say that after the war ended, Jacob returned to Japan as a missionary.

_He recalled how angry he had felt when he learned of the bombing of Pearl Harbor and how that anger had motivated a drive to make the Japanese pay for their actions. Now he marveled that he was in Hawaii on his way back to Japan, not to extract revenge but to tell the people the greatest news Jake had ever heard - the gospel._

The books is well-written and simple enough for children who like to read. Highly recommended!

# [Taming the Tongue](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2025/7/16/taming-the-tongue)

[![Image 8](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/2dc9d856-0bef-4947-9e08-5e3974085f4e/Taming+the+Tongue.jpg)](https://a.co/d/8p82Tc4)

[Taming the Tongue](https://a.co/d/8p82Tc4) is a surprising and wonderful book from our friend Rabbi Dr. Mark Kinzer! Surprising, because it is pastoral, not theological (as most of his books are). Wonderful, because it addresses an important part of community life in a deep, simple, and practical way. So much so, that we’re considering having a book study on it in the future!

Rabbi Kinzer blends considerations from Jewish thought, the Old Testament (including Ecclesiasticus, which is in the Catholic bible but not most Protestant bibles), and the New Testament in this short book. His focus is to help us become aware of ways in which our speech often violates biblical standards (negatively), or doesn’t live up to them (positively).

After an introductory chapter, there are three chapters on speech habits to root out - slander, gossip, and negative humor. They are very challenging! (Even to those of us who have been working on this for decades.)

The final three chapters focus on growing in positive modes of speech - edification, gracious speech, and words of worship and praise. These chapters are also very challenging! Rabbi Kinzer encourages us to not be silent where we are called to speak words that can help our brothers and sisters, or glorify our great God.

The topic in this book is closely related to several aspects of life at CTR we hold dear:

*   George Miley’s teachings on contempt as a sin of violence

*   Caroline Owens’ teaching on The Accuser of the Brethren

*   Our two community rules (both the renunciations and the commitments)

Buy it! Read it! And most of all … practice it!

# [Truth Matters](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2025/4/21/truth-matters)

[![Image 9](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/d70f2bcf-8d2e-4619-bf07-0b9a0ec61166/Truth+Matters.jpg)](https://a.co/d/8Zyw3aW)

The title, subtitle, and the cover image of [Truth Matters](https://a.co/d/8Zyw3aW) say it all. These are two friends, first of all - friends. (Look at the picture!) They are friends who are on different sides of the political discourse that is threatening to divide our nation. And are able to dialogue about their differences in opinion, and of course what they agree on as well, without losing their friendship. And with each admitting they’ve learned a lot from the other.

Dr. George & Dr. West are both professors at Princeton University. They have partnered together to teach a seminar at Princeton, which students clamor to get into because they expect fireworks - given Robert George’s deep conservative credentials, and Cornel West’s equally impressive liberal record. What they get is not what they expect, because rather than arguing reactively against each other, the two eminent professors commend each other as truth-seekers and challenge the students to shed their assumed positions and instead learn from the great writers of Western civilization.

In addition to being conservative & liberal, and White and Black, the two professors are also Catholic and Protestant. And very aware of how they both see the world the same, and also in different ways, due to their engagement in their faith traditions. So their dialogue - and the book really is just a dialogue between then, with an occasional question / topic introduced to guide the conversation - their dialogue is quite relevant to our calling at Christ the Reconciler, in multiple dimensions. For example:

Cornel West: In that sense, Brother Robby’s absolutely right in terms of a truth teller. But truth tellers usually have to be measured by the degree to which they’re willing to tell painful truths about themselves, and then tell painful truths about the group from which they come.

… and …

Robert George: But here’s what we can say and what we should say and what is too rarely said. Often enough people on both sides of hotly contested issues [such as abortion] can and should acknowledge the good faith and goodwill of those who hold different convictions. It is not contradicting the principle of non-contradiction to recognize that there are valid concerns on both sides.

One of our contentions is that building relationships is key to reducing hostility. And sure enough, Chapter 1 of [Truth Matters](https://a.co/d/8Zyw3aW) is about how Dr. George & Dr. West first met, grew to become friends, and decided to teach a class together. The book is worth reading just for the end of this chapter, when they address the question - are they trying to persuade each other, that their views are right. We can all learn much from the humility and affection with which they respond.

I assume if he disagrees with me about something, there’s got to be a pretty good chance I’m wrong about it.  
And I could be wrong too.  
He could be wrong, too.  
Absolutely.

[Loving the Church, Blessing the Nations](https://a.co/d/aPV7nyR) is a special book. The overall theme of the book is to explore how missionary activity can be accomplished in concert with local churches. Historically there has often been conflict between foreign missionaries parachuting into a country with goals and methods that harm, rather than helping, local churches in that country. George Miley draws from his experience on the missions ships Logos and Doulos to describe how they strove to honor local congregations and partner with them, when pulling into a new port somewhere in the world. His stories are wonderful examples of reconciliation and unity at work in the real world, and illustrate Jesus’ genius in connecting world evangelization to church unity in his prayer for us in John 17.

But wait! There’s more!

Hidden in the heart of the book is a stretch of five chapters that stand on their own and have greatly influenced Christ the Reconciler. George introduces the idea of an “apostolically-gifted leader” and addresses these topics:

# [The Final Quest Trilogy](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2024/7/27/the-final-quest-trilogy)

Back in the 1990s, Rick Joyner had a series of immersive visions that he wrote down and published in a small book called _The Final Quest_. A few years later, he added two more volumes - one of related visions since The Final Quest, and the other of earlier visions that he realized were also related. The end result was called [_The Final Quest Trilogy_](https://a.co/d/hlygbuQ).

[![Image 14](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/d24fa1cd-eed7-45c8-a712-b3ad92a45afc/Final+Quest.jpg)](https://a.co/d/hlygbuQ)

Rick makes clear in his introductions to each volume, that the purpose of prophetic visions is not to make doctrine. Scripture is the basis of doctrine, which is not added to by later revelations. However, one purpose of prophecies is to shed light on how God is at work in the times we are in - and this is what he believes the visions of [_The Final Quest Trilogy_](https://a.co/d/hlygbuQ) are for.

This should be a great encouragement to us at CTR, because the importance of unity is a major theme throughout the three books! There are pictures of the divided church that are very helpful, and also wisdom for how to (and how not to) respond to division. Here are three examples, which will hopefully entice you to read the whole book - which everyone who reads it, is deeply impacted by!

*   Wisdom (Jesus) speaking:   
_“My justice does not take sides in human conflicts, even those involving My people … even the greatest saints of the church age have only aligned themselves with My ways a small portion of the time, or with a small part of their minds and hearts. I am not for them or against their enemies, but I am coming to use My people to save their enemies … At this time, even My greatest leaders are seldom in harmony with Me. Many are doing good works, but few are doing what I have called them to do. This is largely the result of divisions among you. I am not coming to take sides with any one group, but I am calling for those who will come over to My side._

*   A description of one scene of the vision, with Wisdom (Jesus) explaining:  
_There was a river in the middle [of the valley] that was fed by streams from every mountain around it. The water sparkled with a blue tint that was the bluest tint I had ever seen and beautifully matched the sky. … “My dwelling places will only be found where all of My streams flow together as one. My builders will come from every stream, but they will work as one.”_

*   A young girl of 10-12 speaking:  
_“It is better to have a few who are in unity than many who are divided, who do not have a single, focused vision. Many of those who were with us before seldom drank from the stream, and I hardly ever heard them pray. I felt they would not last long, and I was right. Such people are more of a detriment when the battle begins.”_

This wonderful, unusual book was written by a good friend and mentor - George Miley. While it certainly can be profitably read solo, it is best suited for a community setting. We love to read it “George Miley style” - which means a small group, seated in a circle, and each person in turns reads one of the numbered paragraphs. A pause for reflection, and the willingness to let that sentence become a springboard to heart-opening discussion, always leads to live-giving conversation. To actually finish the chapter in one go, becomes rare!

The topics George has chosen to cover come from his extensive history in Christian ministry, interlaced with his wide-ranging reading of others who write in the area of formation. Dallas Willard has especially informed George’s thinking and writing. If you find Willard hard to digest, George’s book may be very helpful - to use [Amy’s wonderful analogy for George](https://cogdellcreative.space/w17chs/app3), it’s like he has taken all the mixed up coins in a book such as [_Renovation of the Heart_](https://a.co/d/4KZH2uR), and run them through his orderly coin-sorting-machine mind, so that they come out neatly packaged and easily understood.

These topics include those you may expect …

8 Spiritual Practices  
11 Prayer  
20 Learning How to Forgive

… as well as some that are perhaps unexpected, but important and helpful:

10 How to spend Time in Solitude  
19 Sexuality  
22 Honoring your Father and Mother

And for us, chapter 21, The Ministry of Reconciliation, shows the connection between spiritual formation (our 3rd and central “activity” at Christ the Reconciler”) and reconciliation (our 2nd and titular activity) - so this will be a special chapter of a special book for our community, forever.

# [Contemplating the Trinity](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2023/10/12/contemplating-the-trinity)

[![Image 19](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/7f51dda1-3ffb-46ec-a6a9-0be9f7b5413a/Contemplating+the+Trinity.jpg)](https://a.co/d/90XJ4lU)

As we begin a teaching series this year identifying the “Thick Practice” of our community as **contemplating the Trinity**, we may wonder - where did that phrase come from? The answer is this book: [Contemplating the Trinity](https://a.co/d/90XJ4lU), by Fr. Raniero Cantalamessa.

For those of you not familiar with Fr. Cantalamessa, he is an important figure in the Catholic Church. He has been the preacher to the papal household since 1980! A leader in the Catholic Charismatic movement, Cantalamessa is also a prolific author, writing well-known books such as _The Sober Intoxication of the Spirit_ (one of those books that blesses you just by reading the title!)

_Contemplating the Trinity_ was first published in Italian in 2002, and translated into English in 2007. The book begins with a series of three icons that portray the Trinity - first among them the Rublev icon that has been so important to us at Christ the Reconciler. As is appropriate for that beginning, Cantalamessa begins with an exploration of the Trinity in Eastern thought - after all, the Nicene Creed is a gift to the global church primarily from our Eastern Orthodox brothers and sisters, whose tradition explores the depths of the mystery of the Trinity.

From there the topics that Fr. Cantalamessa explores include prayer, beauty, and communion - all highly relevant to our life and vision at Christ the Reconciler. This is a great book to read in this season of our life, and return to frequently as part of our “Thick Practice” in years to come.

# [At the Foot of the Mountain](http://www.christthereconciler.org/book-of-the-month/2023/6/27/at-the-foot-of-the-mountain)

This intriguing book began as a conversation via email between two Messianic Jews. One, Jen Rosner, advocates for the newly emerging Messianic Jewish movement to consider valuing consistently Torah-observant lifestyles. Her brother-in-law, Josh Lessard, while not opposed to Torah observance, believes that individual Messianic Jews should prioritize the leading of the Spirit.

[![Image 20](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/52912fcee4b0de25af3126b9/184965ae-38c7-4721-911e-6dabcd425607/Foot+Of+the+Mountain.jpg)](https://www.amazon.com/At-Foot-Mountain-Views-Spirit/dp/1666700630/ref=cm_cr_arp_d_product_top?ie=UTF8)

There are many reasons to recommend reading [At the Foot of the Mountain](https://www.amazon.com/At-Foot-Mountain-Views-Spirit/dp/1666700630/ref=cm_cr_arp_d_product_top?ie=UTF8). First and foremost is the irenic spirit with which the conversation is conducted. While being direct about their disagreements, Jen and Josh respect each other and seek to honor one another throughout the book. This provides a helpful corrective to the all-too-common hostility with which brothers and sisters in Christ argue in books, on social media, and in podcasts.

Another area of strength is the depth of thought that each gives to their discussions. Jen is coming from more of an academic perspective. Josh, a rabbi for a Messianic Jewish synagogue, takes a pastoral approach. Each of them is well read, have studied scriptures deeply, and present their arguments with clarity and even humor.

Finally, an area of interest for our community - which has many Catholics - is the applicability of this discussion to ongoing conversations in the Roman Catholic church. Some advocate that following the rules of the Catholic Church create a distinct people that displays the beauty of Christ on the earth. Others believe a more Spirit-led approach can lead Catholics to discern when and how to best adhere to the heart of Roman Catholicism. The conversation between Jen and Josh may shed light on this discussion, but from the helpfully oblique angle of Messianic Judaism.
