_**What's So Amazing About Grace?**_ is a 1997 book by [Philip Yancey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Yancey "Philip Yancey"), an American journalist and editor-at-large for _[Christianity Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity\_Today "Christianity Today")_. The book examines [grace in Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_in_Christianity "Grace in Christianity"), contending that people crave grace and that it is central to [the gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_gospel "The gospel"), but that many local churches ignore grace and instead seek to exterminate [immorality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immorality "Immorality"). _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ includes [Bible stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_story "Bible story"), anecdotes from Yancey's life, accounts of historical events and other stories. These include a modern retelling of the [Parable of the Prodigal Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Prodigal_Son "Parable of the Prodigal Son"), an account of Yancey's friendship with [Mel White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_White "Mel White") who [came out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out") as gay, a comparison of the teachings of [early Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Christianity "Early Christianity")[Pelagius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagius "Pelagius") and [Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo "Augustine of Hippo"), and a summary of [Karen Blixen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Blixen "Karen Blixen")'s short story "[Babette's Feast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anecdotes_of_Destiny "Anecdotes of Destiny")".

Yancey was inspired to write _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ after President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") asked him, "Why do Christians hate so much?"[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Briggs-1) Although Yancey initially intended to call the book _What's So Amazing About Grace: and Why Don't Christians Show More of It?_, [Zondervan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zondervan "Zondervan"), its publisher, objected to this title despite the author's contention that he wrote the book to communicate the belief that grace is one of the best quality Christians, like himself, have to offer but are not necessarily identified with it.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Waterloo-2) The book was successful at secular and Christian stores, selling more than 15 million copies by 2006 and becoming Yancey's best-known book. In it, Yancey coined the phrase "scandal of grace", referring to the idea that God forgives some of the worst people, citing the [conversion of Paul the Apostle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_of_Paul_the_Apostle "Conversion of Paul the Apostle").

_What's So Amazing About Grace?_ was named Book of the Year by the [Evangelical Christian Publishers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Christian_Publishers_Association "Evangelical Christian Publishers Association") in 1998. In 2006, it ranked 17th on _Christianity Today_'s list of fifty books that have shaped [Evangelicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism "Evangelicalism") the most. In a _[Publishers Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers\_Weekly "Publishers Weekly")_ review, Henry Carrigan notes an anecdotal style that can be frustrating but ultimately worth reading. For the _[Presbyterian Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian\_Record "Presbyterian Record")_, Canadian Christian writer [Phil Callaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Callaway "Phil Callaway") writes that he found the book refreshing and inspirational. _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ has been endorsed by a number of public figures, including Irish musician [Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono "Bono"), British adventurer [Debra Searle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debra_Searle "Debra Searle"), and [World Vision Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Vision_Australia "World Vision Australia") CEO [Tim Costello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Costello "Tim Costello").

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 6: Bill Clinton and his dog Buddy](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Clinton_Buddy_120597.jpg/250px-Clinton_Buddy_120597.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clinton_Buddy_120597.jpg)

[Philip Yancey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Yancey "Philip Yancey") was inspired by [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") (pictured here, 1997) to write the book.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Briggs-1)

[Philip Yancey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Yancey "Philip Yancey"), an American journalist[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Daily-3) based in Colorado,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Winnipeg-4) was inspired to write a book about [grace in Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_in_Christianity "Grace in Christianity") when he went to the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") to interview President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"). Clinton, a [Southern Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Baptist_Convention "Southern Baptist Convention") from birth, told him, "I've been in politics long enough to expect criticism and hostility. But I was unprepared for the hatred I get from Christians. Why do Christians hate so much?"[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Briggs-1) Yancey later said that, although there are many reasons for [Evangelical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism "Evangelicalism") Christians to disapprove of [Clinton's policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clintonism "Clintonism") and lifestyle, hating him was not a valid option for Christians.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Briggs-1)

The author was further prompted to write about grace when a friend told him about encountering a homeless prostitute in Chicago who began to cry as she told him that she had raised money for drugs by [prostituting her two-year-old child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostitution_of_children "Prostitution of children"). When Yancey's friend asked the woman if she had sought help at a local church, she answered, "Church? Why would I ever go there? I was already feeling terrible about myself. They'd just make me feel worse."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Atlanta-5) This story convinced Yancey that Christians are doing a poor job of communicating the message that God is willing to accept people, regardless of what they have done; the story haunted him, he said, because the woman was "the type of person who would have gone to Jesus. The more unrighteous a person was, the more comfortable they felt around Jesus".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Atlanta-5)

Yancey researched the subject of grace, asking non-Christians what they associated with Evangelical Christianity. None of their responses mentioned grace; most cited political stances, such as [opposition to LGBT rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_opposition "LGBT rights opposition") and [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_pro-life_movement "United States pro-life movement").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) The author initially intended to call his book _What's So Amazing About Grace: and Why Don't Christians Show More of It?_[Zondervan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zondervan "Zondervan"), its eventual publisher, objected to the title's forcefulness, despite Yancey's argument that he wrote the book about how "we Christians are simply not known by the greatest gift we have".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Waterloo-2) On February 3, 1997, _[Christianity Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity\_Today "Christianity Today")_ published an essay by Yancey, the magazine's editor-at-large,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Science-7) with the title "A State of Ungrace", saying that it was the basis of two chapters of Yancey's upcoming book with the [working title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_title "Working title") of _What's So Amazing About Grace and Why the World Needs More of It_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Yancey-8) The book was published later that year with the shorter title _What's So Amazing About Grace?_[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYancey1997-9)

[![Image 7: Philip Yancey](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Philip_Yancey.jpg/250px-Philip_Yancey.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philip_Yancey.jpg)

Although Yancey _(pictured, 2014)_ has written several international bestsellers, _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ is his best-known.

According to the author, he began writing the book in the same way he began most of his books: by exploring a question that was unresolved for him. In this case, the question became the book's title.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-10) In _What's So Amazing About Grace?_, Yancey answers this question by writing that God gives grace to people unconditionally, without their need to earn it. His book includes [Bible stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_story "Bible story"), [anecdotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anecdote "Anecdote") from Yancey's life and accounts of historical events.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Carrigan-11) Similar to his other works, _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ has a [self-deprecating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-deprecation "Self-deprecation") tone.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Christianity-12) It describes Yancey's upbringing in a [judgmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_judgment "Value judgment") church, a theme Yancey previously explored in _[The Jesus I Never Knew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jesus\_I\_Never\_Knew "The Jesus I Never Knew")_ and later returned to in _[Reaching for the Invisible God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaching\_for\_the\_Invisible\_God "Reaching for the Invisible God")_ and _[Soul Survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul\_Survivor\_(book) "Soul Survivor (book)")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Winnipeg-4)

_What's So Amazing About Grace?_ sold well at secular and Christian stores.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Today-13) Its popularity in the United Kingdom grew in 2003, when the impending [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") boosted sales of religious literature in the country. That March, it was the seventh-bestselling religious book in the UK, behind [Rick Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Warren "Rick Warren")'s _[The Purpose Driven Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Purpose\_Driven\_Life "The Purpose Driven Life")_, [John Ortberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ortberg "John Ortberg")'s _[If You Want to Walk on Water, You've Got to Get Out of the Boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If\_You\_Want\_to\_Walk\_on\_Water,\_You've\_Got\_to\_Get\_Out\_of\_the\_Boat "If You Want to Walk on Water, You've Got to Get Out of the Boat")_ and [Eugene H. Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_H._Peterson "Eugene H. Peterson")'s _[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Message\_(Bible) "The Message (Bible)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-14)_What's So Amazing About Grace?_ is Yancey's best-known book, having sold more than 15 million copies by 2006.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-15) Initially, the book was especially popular among [baby boomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_boomers "Baby boomers").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-16) Its popularity helped increase sales of Yancey's 2000 book _Reaching for the Invisible God_, which appeared on religion bestseller lists immediately after publication.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-17)_What's So Amazing About Grace?_ is one of several books by Yancey that have become international bestsellers.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-18)

## Content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Content")]

> Grace did not come to me initially in the forms or the words of faith. I grew up in a church that often used the word but meant something else. ... I became a writer, I feel certain, in an attempt to reclaim words that had been tarnished by graceless Christians.

—Yancey, pages 41-42.

In _What's So Amazing About Grace?_, Yancey discusses grace, calling it "our last best word".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetweiler200855-19) The book's thesis is that, although people crave grace and it is centrally important to [the gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_gospel "The gospel"), many local churches ignore grace in their quest to exterminate [immorality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immorality "Immorality"). Yancey uses the word "ungrace" to describe actions that fail to demonstrate grace.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Science-7) According to the author, the greatest gift the [Christian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Church "Christian Church") can give the world is grace, but the church sometimes offers ungrace instead.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Free-20) Yancey writes that there are secular analogues to most Christian activities benefiting the world, such as [social justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_justice "Social justice") work and [community service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_service "Community service"), but that "grace is theological; it comes from God. It's one thing the church can offer that isn't found anywhere else".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Waterloo-2) He describes his experiences attempting to make grace part of the way he lived and not just part of his theology. Yancey quotes [Christian counselor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_counseling "Christian counseling")[David Seamands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Seamands "David Seamands"): "The two major causes of most emotional problems among Evangelical Christians are these: the failure to understand, receive and live out God's unconditional grace and forgiveness; and the failure to give out that unconditional love, forgiveness, and grace to other people".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetweiler200855-19)

The author describes his experiences growing up in a church that, despite preaching about grace, did not demonstrate it to others; the church excluded African Americans, dismissed other Christians on the basis of slightly different beliefs, and depicted God as tyrannical and vengeful.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Winnipeg-4) Yancey writes, "I grew up with the strong impression that a person became spiritual by attending to grey-area rules," and that church was a place to look good rather than be honest.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) He contrasts the teachings of [early Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Christianity "Early Christianity")[Pelagius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagius "Pelagius") and [Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo "Augustine of Hippo") on the subject of grace, with Pelagius believing that [divine grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_grace "Divine grace") must be earned and Augustine contending that grace is a gift that cannot be earned. Pelagius was declared a [heretic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heresy "Heresy") by his peers; Augustine was [canonized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization "Canonization"). According to Yancey, many Christians follow Pelagius's teaching on grace during the week but espouse Augustine's on Sunday.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Waterloo-2)

Yancey writes that Christians should be politically active and should, for example, [oppose abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion_movements "Anti-abortion movements"), "but you have to find a way to do it with grace... If I'm against abortion and I don't find a way to love the woman who got the abortion and even her doctor, then I don't understand the gospel."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Atlanta-5) Yancey recounts Jesus's [Parable of the Unforgiving Servant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Unforgiving_Servant "Parable of the Unforgiving Servant"), concluding that God is only willing to forgive us if we are willing to forgive those who have wronged us. In a similar vein, he quotes [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare")'s _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice "The Merchant of Venice")_: "How shalt thou hope for mercy, rendering none?"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMousley20071-21)

The author summarizes [Karen Blixen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Blixen "Karen Blixen")'s short story "[Babette's Feast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anecdotes_of_Destiny "Anecdotes of Destiny")", which was [adapted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_adaptation "Film adaptation") into [a 1987 Danish film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babette's_Feast "Babette's Feast"). The story is set in a fishing village where the inhabitants avoid all pleasure for religious reasons.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2015175-22) Two sisters take in Babette, a Parisian refugee who becomes their personal chef, but they allow her to make only simple, bland meals. Years pass; Babette wins a lottery and spends her winnings on a delicious banquet for the villagers, who agree to eat but not enjoy the food.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2015176-23) A banquet guest recognizes Babette as a former world-renowned chef and identifies her gift to undeserving and initially unwilling recipients as grace.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2015177-24) In another chapter Yancey similarly summarizes [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Garc%C3%ADa_M%C3%A1rquez "Gabriel García Márquez")'s novel _[Love in the Time of Cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love\_in\_the\_Time\_of\_Cholera "Love in the Time of Cholera")_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Olson-25)

[![Image 8: Mel White](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Mel_white_christmas.jpg/250px-Mel_white_christmas.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mel_white_christmas.jpg)

Yancey writes about his friendship with prominent pastor [Mel White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_White "Mel White")_(pictured, 1995)_.

Yancey describes his friendship with [Mel White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_White "Mel White"), who was a married pastor and [Fuller Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuller_Theological_Seminary "Fuller Theological Seminary") lecturer with two children when he [came out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out") as gay. White had been a [ghostwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostwriter "Ghostwriter") for Christian writers including [Francis Schaeffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Schaeffer "Francis Schaeffer"), [Billy Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Graham "Billy Graham") and [Jerry Falwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Falwell "Jerry Falwell"), and Yancey was surprised by White's self-disclosure. According to the author, he and White had long discussions on the subject "because he wanted so much for me to approve. I couldn't approve."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) Yancey writes that, although he continued to cultivate his friendship with White, many other Christians shunned the pastor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) One chapter, "The Lovesick Father", retells the [Parable of the Prodigal Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Prodigal_Son "Parable of the Prodigal Son") in a modern setting with the spendthrift child, a daughter.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Carrigan-11) Yancey writes that the closest many people get to experiencing pure grace is a [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_(love) "Romance (love)") relationship, when they believe that "someone at last feels that I — I! — am the most desirable, attractive, companionable creature on the planet".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Atlanta-5)

## Influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Influence")]

Christians of many [denominations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_denomination "Christian denomination") treat _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ as a [handbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handbook "Handbook"). In it, Yancey [coined the phrase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neologism "Neologism") "scandal of grace", referring to the idea that God may choose to forgive people who have done evil deeds, citing the [conversion of Paul the Apostle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_of_Paul_the_Apostle "Conversion of Paul the Apostle") who was [persecuting Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Christians "Persecution of Christians"). The phrase "scandal of grace" has become widely used in Christian circles.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-26) In 2005, [the Barna Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Barna_Group "The Barna Group"), a California-based research firm, asked senior pastors across the United States which books they had found helpful during the past three years. _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ was one of nine books mentioned by at least two percent of the respondents; the other eight included Rick Warren's _[The Purpose Driven Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Purpose\_Driven\_Church "The Purpose Driven Church")_ and _The Purpose Driven Life_ and [John C. Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Maxwell "John C. Maxwell")'s _[The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_21\_Irrefutable\_Laws\_of\_Leadership "The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership")_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-27)

[David Charlesworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Charlesworth "David Charlesworth"), [Abbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbot "Abbot") of [Buckfast Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckfast_Abbey "Buckfast Abbey") in Devon, England, asked [Torbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torbay "Torbay")-based theatre company Unleashed Productions to perform a play based on the book. The play had been written by Neil Pugmire and previously performed in 2006 at the Greenbelt Festival. It incorporated stories about [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid"), [Gordon Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Wilson_(peace_campaigner) "Gordon Wilson (peace campaigner)")'s daughter's death in the [Remembrance Day bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remembrance_Day_bombing "Remembrance Day bombing"), and [Holocaust survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Holocaust_survivors "List of Holocaust survivors")[Simon Wiesenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Wiesenthal "Simon Wiesenthal"). He also included a dramatization of the chapter "The Lovesick Father". Simon Zimmerman wrote the score for the play, which has a cast of nearly forty actors. The play, which took the name of the book, was successfully produced outdoors by Buckfast Abbey in 2010.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Western-28) These outdoor performances were well-attended.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-29) According to the _[Western Morning News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western\_Morning\_News "Western Morning News")_, the play is "by turns shocking, humorous and moving, [and] explores how forgiveness and grace can be found in even the most testing circumstances".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Western-28) A _[Herald Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torquay\_Herald\_Express "Torquay Herald Express")_ reviewer called the play inspiring and probably the most unique and unusual in [South Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Devon "South Devon") that summer.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Herald-30)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Secular media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Secular media")]

[![Image 9: A scene from a 19th-century performance of The Merchant of Venice](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Jacob_Adler_as_Shylock.jpg/250px-Jacob_Adler_as_Shylock.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacob_Adler_as_Shylock.jpg)

Yancey quotes [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare")'s play _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice "The Merchant of Venice")_ in _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ _(relevant scene pictured)_; according to Shakespearean scholar Andy Mousley, the quotation demonstrates Yancey's [moral universalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_universalism "Moral universalism").

For _[Booklist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booklist "Booklist")_, Ray Olson called _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ a "well-written and engaging book [that] will continue to nourish readers' hunger for spiritual sustenance long after it has answered the appetites of an initial burst of consumers".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Olson-25) He compared the book to [Max Lucado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Lucado "Max Lucado")'s _[The Great House of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Great\_House\_of\_God "The Great House of God")_, also published in 1997, writing that, although Yancey and Lucado have both written several bestselling [Christian books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_literature "Christian literature"), Yancey's book was edited better. Olson praised as pithy the author's summaries of "Babette's Feast" and _Love in the Time of Cholera_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Olson-25) In the _[Calgary Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary\_Herald "Calgary Herald")_, David Briggs compares _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ to [Johann Christoph Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Christoph_Arnold "Johann Christoph Arnold")'s _Seventy Times Seven: The Power of Forgiveness_, also published in 1997; according to both books, Christians should be more [charitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charity_(virtue) "Charity (virtue)") to others and less judgmental of them.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Briggs-1) Henry Carrigan writes in his _[Publishers Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers\_Weekly "Publishers Weekly")_ review that "the book's anecdotal style is often frustrating, but Yancey's measured prose and his insights into the stories make the book worth reading".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Carrigan-11) In her 1998 _[Winnipeg Free Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg\_Free\_Press "Winnipeg Free Press")_ review, Karen Toole-Mitchell criticizes Yancey's contention that everyone needs grace and that Christians have a special ability to offer it. She calls Yancey's grace "cheap... because it was not needed, it was not felt, and ultimately it was not received".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Free-20)

In the _[Coventry Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry\_Telegraph "Coventry Telegraph")_ in 2001, Barbara Goulden called the book's title provocative.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-31) A 2003 _[Daily Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Express "Daily Express")_ review called _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ "a cogent, intellectually robust defence of [Christianity] without all the crap that goes with so many churches today".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Daily-3) Derick Bingham of the _[Belfast Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast\_Telegraph "Belfast Telegraph")_ recommended the book that year, calling it a liberating read.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-32) In 2006, Terry Pluto of the _[Akron Beacon Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron\_Beacon\_Journal "Akron Beacon Journal")_ called _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ and the earlier _[Disappointment with God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disappointment\_with\_God "Disappointment with God")_ Yancey's best books.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-33)

Shakespearean scholar Andy Mousley called the book part of the "spiritual self-help genre" in 2007. According to Mousley, Yancey's quotation from _The Merchant of Venice_ demonstrates the author's [moral universalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_universalism "Moral universalism"); Yancey views Shakespeare as a sage who conveyed universally applicable morals, a perspective contradicting most contemporary [literary critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_criticism "Literary criticism") who distrust moral universalism, using [historicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicism "Historicism") to contextualize [Shakespeare's religious views](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_views_of_William_Shakespeare "Religious views of William Shakespeare").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMousley20071-21) Dean Poling of _[The Valdosta Daily Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Valdosta\_Daily\_Times "The Valdosta Daily Times")_ wrote in 2008 that, in _What's So Amazing About Grace?_, "Yancey writes about faith in a clear, honest, and inquisitive style" consistent with his other books.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-34) In 2010, a _Herald Express_ journalist called the book "hardhitting" and "gritty".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Herald-30)

### Christian media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Christian media")]

[![Image 10: John Newton](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/John_Newton.jpg/250px-John_Newton.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Newton.jpg)

In _The Christian Science Monitor_, Karla Vallance calls the book similarly sentimental to the hymn "Amazing Grace" by John Newton _(pictured)_.

_What's So Amazing About Grace?_ was named Book of the Year by the [Evangelical Christian Publishers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Christian_Publishers_Association "Evangelical Christian Publishers Association") in 1998 when it was chosen by Christian retailers as the title they most enjoyed selling;[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-35) Yancey's _The Jesus I Never Knew_ had received the same award two years earlier.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-36) In 1998, _Christianity Today_ compared _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ to Joel A. Carpenter's _Revive Us Again_, writing that both books productively analyze [Christian fundamentalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_fundamentalism "Christian fundamentalism").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Today-13) That year, Karla Vallance's _[Christian Science Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Christian\_Science\_Monitor "The Christian Science Monitor")_ review called the book similarly sentimental to [John Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Newton "John Newton")'s [hymn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn "Hymn") "[Amazing Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing_Grace "Amazing Grace")".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-37)

In a 1998 _[Presbyterian Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian\_Record "Presbyterian Record")_ review, Canadian Christian writer [Phil Callaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Callaway "Phil Callaway") writes that _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ made him "thankful afresh for God's grace and challenged to live a life reflecting it".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) Callaway was haunted by Yancey's question, "If grace is so amazing, why don't Christians show more of it?"[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) and expressed his appreciation to the author at the 1998 [Christian Booksellers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBA_(Christian_trade_association) "CBA (Christian trade association)") convention. When he asked Yancey why he wrote the book, the author answered: "I long for the church to become a culture of grace... A graceful church knows how to welcome failure and rewards vulnerability so that a person automatically thinks of the church when needing help."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) Yancey asked Callaway if he thought the book would generate controversy, and Callaway said it would. Callaway asked Yancey why his book was so harsh in its description of Christians, and Yancey responded, "I'm picking on Christians because I am one".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6) Yancey said that he knew many gracious Christians and that secular culture was filled with examples of ungrace, including media manipulation of [body image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_image "Body image") and the belief that "[there ain't no such thing as a free lunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There_ain't_no_such_thing_as_a_free_lunch "There ain't no such thing as a free lunch")", which contradicts the concept of undeserved grace from God as taught in Christianity.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Callaway-6)

A 1999 _Christian Science Monitor_ review said that, filled with "poignant stories" that are "likely to ruffle some feathers, this compelling book challenges Christians to become a genuine healing force in society".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Science-7)[Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") pastor [John Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Buchanan_(pastor) "John Buchanan (pastor)"), editor and publisher of _[The Christian Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Christian\_Century "The Christian Century")_, also reviewed _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ that year, writing that "Yancey is such a good writer and such a generous evangelical that even though I occasionally disagree with his conclusions, I'm glad to be in the same family with him".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-38)

[![Image 11: Robert Jeffress](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Robert_Jeffress.jpg/250px-Robert_Jeffress.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Jeffress.jpg)

[Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptists "Baptists") pastor [Robert Jeffress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jeffress "Robert Jeffress") said that _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ "did a valuable service rescuing the doctrine of grace from the legalists who say that we must earn our salvation".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Guthrie-39)

In 2006, _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ placed 17th on _Christianity Today_'s list of fifty books that had most shaped Evangelicals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Christianity-12) That year, [Robert Jeffress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jeffress "Robert Jeffress"), pastor of [First Baptist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Baptist_Church_(Dallas) "First Baptist Church (Dallas)") in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), compared _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ to [Chuck Swindoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Swindoll "Chuck Swindoll")'s book _The Grace Awakening_, calling both "wonderful books on grace [that] did a valuable service rescuing the doctrine of grace from the legalists who say that we must earn our salvation".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Guthrie-39) Christian professor [Craig Detweiler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Detweiler "Craig Detweiler") writes in his 2008 book _A Purple State of Mind: Finding Middle Ground in a Divided Culture_ that, if he could have given his students a graduation present, it would have been a copy of _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ because many of his Christian students were more concerned with avoiding the forbidden than they were with enjoying the permitted. Detweiler writes that Christianity was founded on forgiveness and that Christians should not bear the burden of guilt, and he therefore agrees with Yancey that "grace" is "our last best word".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetweiler200855-19)

In a 2014 article in the "Spiritual Matters" section of the Australian newspaper _[The Daily Examiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Examiner "The Daily Examiner")_, Reverend Chris Sparks calls _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ "masterful" and writes that Yancey provides a good answer to the question raised by its title.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-40) In his 2015 book _Unoffendable: How Just One Change Can Make All of Life Better_, Christian radio personality [Brant Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brant_Hansen "Brant Hansen") calls _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ life-changing and writes that Yancey's discussion of "Babette's Feast" inspired him to see the film.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2015175-22)_[U.S. Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claretians#Publications "Claretians")_ reviewer Mary Lynn Hendrickson also praised Yancey's retelling of Karen Blixen's story.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-41)

### Public figures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=What%27s_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Public figures")]

[![Image 12: Debra Searle](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Debra_Searle_MVO%2C_MBE_portrait_photo_with_oar_by_Hayley_Barnard.jpg/250px-Debra_Searle_MVO%2C_MBE_portrait_photo_with_oar_by_Hayley_Barnard.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Debra_Searle_MVO,_MBE_portrait_photo_with_oar_by_Hayley_Barnard.jpg)

[Atlantic Rowing Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Rowing_Race "Atlantic Rowing Race") participant [Debra Searle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debra_Searle "Debra Searle") read Yancey's book during her [transatlantic crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_crossing "Transatlantic crossing"), later crediting it with her return to Christianity.

In 2000, [Bear Grylls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Grylls "Bear Grylls"), the youngest [Briton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_people "British people") to survive an ascent of [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), cited _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ as his "favourite holiday read"[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-42) and "a book that has inspired me a lot".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-43) In 2001, American politician [Mark Earley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Earley "Mark Earley") called it his favorite book.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-44) That year, English musician [Noel Gallagher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Gallagher "Noel Gallagher") asked Irish musician [Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono "Bono") to explain religion to him because Gallagher knew Bono believed in and prayed to God. Bono spoke with Gallagher on the subject for two hours and sent him a copy of _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ Gallagher later said that he was "going to have a good read of this book", that Bono "made a lot of sense", and that the gift was particularly meaningful because Bono's father had recently died.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-45)

During Christmas 2001, while [Debra Searle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debra_Searle "Debra Searle") was competing in the [Atlantic Rowing Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Rowing_Race "Atlantic Rowing Race") by making a solo [transatlantic crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_crossing "Transatlantic crossing") from [Tenerife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenerife "Tenerife") to Barbados, her twin sister Hayley sent her a copy of _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ as part of a Christmas package that was delivered at sea. Although she had belonged to a local church as a child, Debra had become [irreligious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion "Irreligion") by 2001. After reading Yancey's book while she was alone on the ocean that Christmas, she said, "I felt like God was there with me protecting me".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Success-46) Reading the book brought about a change in her that eventually resulted in her becoming actively involved in Mutley Baptist Church, which is noted for its [community engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_engagement "Community engagement").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-Success-46)

In 2006, Welsh musician [Mal Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Pope "Mal Pope") called the book his favorite, comparing Yancey's writing to that of British [Christian apologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_apologetics "Christian apologetics")[C. S. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._S._Lewis "C. S. Lewis") and saying, "The first time I read [_What's So Amazing About Grace?_] I ended up in tears with every new chapter".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-47) In 2012, Pope affirmed that it was still his favorite book.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-48)[Tim Costello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Costello "Tim Costello"), CEO of [World Vision Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Vision_Australia "World Vision Australia"), said in 2008 that the book was important to him.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-49) In 2010, American politician [Bill Haslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Haslam "Bill Haslam") cited _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ and [John Heilemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Heilemann "John Heilemann")'s and [Mark Halperin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Halperin "Mark Halperin")'s _[Game Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Change "Game Change")_ as two recent books he enjoyed.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-50) Retired [Northern Ireland Civil Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Civil_Service "Northern Ireland Civil Service") head [Nigel Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Hamilton_(civil_servant) "Nigel Hamilton (civil servant)") said in 2014 that _What's So Amazing About Grace?_ was his favorite book.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_So_Amazing_About_Grace%3F#cite_note-51)

[![Image 4: Amazing Grace by Kathleen Norris book review](https://pollycastor.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/0.jpg)](https://pollycastor.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/0.jpg)

I agree with this author’s dismay over the colossal amount of baggage spiritual terminology has. This is especially true for me who wasn’t brought up with it, but was even true for this author who strayed and then returned to it. I love how candid she is about her experience and how much room she encourages us all to give these words.

This is not a new book (1999) and I found it last summer when I was doing a book purge of my office. I had not yet read it but liked previous work by this author. So last July, I started reading this a chapter every couple of days, a pace which I felt contributed largely to my enjoyment of the book.

Kathleen Norris is a poet and as such writes incredibly well. She can cut directly and incisively to the heart of something, and she can also take the long way around spiraling in on her point. This journey with her coming back to the Presbyterian church, via needed nourishment from Benedictine nuns, is soul expanding to read.

Each chapter tackles a word used in faith circles, like redemption, sin, prayer, antichrist, grace, unchurched, chosen, theology, asceticism, pentecostal, trinity, mystic, creeds, blood, repentance, righteousness, annunciation, salvation, detachment, belief, doubt, intolerance, worship, hell, apocalypse, and many more.

Not surprisingly, I loved some chapters, and others did not care that much about. Because of this, it probably reflects more of my unevenness than the author’s, that I give this book four stars. It would be great to read together with a group to discuss the ideas further, and our book group has slated it for February to do just that.

Here are the bits that stood out to me, although these quotes lose a bit of their punch out of context:

*   “To say ‘yes’ is to make a leap of faith, to risk oneself in a new and often scary relationship.”
*   “I was startled by the words that had come flying out of my mouth; as so often happens when I am put on the spot, I had said things I hadn’t fully realized were true until I’d said them.”
*   “Our words are wiser than we are.”
*   “What the pastor said was so simple that it will remain with me forever. ‘Each of us acts as the anti-Christ,’ he said, ‘whenever we hear the gospel and do not do it.”
*   Silence liberates the imagination. “Silence reminds me to take my soul with me wherever I go.”
*   “The Hebrew word for salvation means literally ‘to make wide,’ or to ‘make sufficient.'”
*   “Paul makes it clear that if we take inordinate pride in the spiritual gifts we have been blessed with, the joke is on us.”
*   “One sixth-century monk, Dorotheus of Gaza, describes detachment as being free from wanting certain things to happen, and remaining so trusting of God that what is happening will be the thing you want and you will be at peace with all.”
*   “Conversion is a process; it is not a goal, not a product we consume… Conversion is no more spectacular than learning to love the people we live with and work among. Conversion is seeing ourselves, and the ordinary people in our families, our classrooms, and on the job in a new light.”
*   “Addictions and their aftermath take people to the depths of evil…Admitting to addiction often makes people humble, less willing to trust in their self-will alone. And that, the desert monks would say, is half the battle.”
*   “Who has not felt the sudden lifting of what had seemed an unbearable burden, the removal of what for too long had been an insurmountable obstacle? Who does not have something deep within that they would not wish to exorcise, so that it no longer casts a shadow on their capacity to receive and give love?”
*   “Perfectionism is one of the scariest words I know… The word that has been translated as ‘perfect’ does not mean to set forth an impossible goal, or the perfectionism that would have me strive for it at any cost. It is taken from a Latin word meaning complete, entire, full-grown. To those who originally heard it, the word would convey ‘mature’ rather than what we mean today by ‘perfect… Maturity for one person is different from maturity for another… This sort of perfection demands that we become fully ourselves as God would have us: mature, ripe, full, ready for what befalls us, for whatever is to come.'”
*   “Receive a guest with the same attitude you have when you are alone; when alone; maintain alone the same attitude you have in receiving guests.”
*   “Prayer is not asking for what you think you want but asking to be changed in ways you can’t imagine.”
*   “At its Greek root, ‘to believe’ simply means ‘to give one’s heart to.’ Thus, if we can determine what it is we give our heart to, then we will know what it is we believe.”
*   “I had thought my doubts were spectacular obstacles to my faith and was confused but intrigued when an old monk blithely stated that doubt is merely the seed of faith, a sign that faith is alive and ready to grow.”
*   “It took me a long time to recognize that the desire to worship is in itself a significant form of belief.”
*   “ambivalence is a sacred emotion.”
*   “When the mystery of God’s love breaks through into my consciousness, do I run from it?… Or am I virgin enough to respond from my deepest, truest self, and say something new, a ‘yes’ that will change me forever?”
*   Jung knew that what we reject as ‘nothing’ always gets us in the end.”
*   “Idolatry makes love impossible.”
*   “Unfortunately it is scorn for others that often marks religion’s public face in America.”
*   “Righteous: at its root in Hebrew, the words means ‘one whose aim is true,'”
*   “Hope may be a kind of name for God.”
*   “God is identified through relationship. One that demands great willingness to trust and to take risks.”
*   “Thomas Aquinas said that God was active, always in motion– an ocean of being, the sun lighting up the atmosphere; not a noun, but a verb. The-God-Who-Is,’
*   “I have come to think of Mary as the patron saint of ‘both/and’ passion over ‘either/or’ reasoning… as simultaneously Virgin and Mother.”
*   “I wonder if holiness is not the ability to apply one’s anger in quietly working against systemic evil, taking care not to draw undue attention to oneself.”
*   “When it is absolutely necessary to correct another, do so, they said. But do it quickly and simply, then let it go. Don’t get entangled in the expectation of results.”
*   “Much if not most intolerance is at base a stupefying ignorance rather than a deeply rooted conviction.”
*   “Jesus Christ asks us to interpret ourselves, and each other, with the same hospitable, good-hearted diligence that we grant to him. He offers the truth not as a thing but as a way, an opening on the path between the spirit and the letter of the law– a way of forbearance.”
*   “It seems to me that if you can’t ever admit to being a wretch, you haven’t been paying attention.”
*   “Faith is best thought of as a verb, not a ‘thing’ that either you have or you don’t.”
*   “Faith is not synonymous with certainty but is the decision to keep your eyes open.”
*   “Faith then is fragile, something that needs tending.”
*   “Church is about community loving their neighbor as themselves. You go because someone may need you there.”
*   “Worship itself might in fact be a living poem.”
*   “When God-talk is speech that is not of this world, it is a false language.”
*   “Political power seems to corrupt religions, corroding them from within.”
*   “I often think that if I’m a Christian, I’ll be the last to know.”
*   The Rule of St. Benedict states that “all guests who present themselves are to be welcomed as Christ. Benedict knew that hospitality could be life-saving for both monk and guest. He instructs Benedictines not to turn their backs on the world, even as they seek to detach themselves from worldly values. To reject the world is to reject other people, and to reject other people is to reject Christ himself.”
*   “Mary knows that no small part of welcoming a guest is the ability to settle down and listen.”
*   “No woman gives birth to an enemy face.”
*   “The story of Jacob says to me that if we’ve ever truly been forgiven, we have seen the face of God. If we’ve ever been on the receiving end of an act of mercy that made a difference in our lives, we have seen the face of God.”
*   “People who have endured the pain of exile and enslavement are likely to take refuge in the thought that there is punishment for their tormentors, if not in this world then in the next.”
*   “The word ‘apocalypse’ comes from the Greek for ‘uncovering’ or ‘revealing,’ which makes it a word of possibilities.”
*   “When people speak in the same tone of voice about a ‘personal deodorant,’ a ‘personal trainer.’ and a ‘personal Savior,’ I suspect what they really mean is private. (I’ve got mine; too bad about you.) but Christianity, like its ancestor Judaism, is inescapably communal.”
*   “Dogma is not dogmatic dogmatism. The Greek root from which dogma comes means “what seems good, fitting, and becoming.'”
*   “The reality of human sin is admitted, but the sin of casting judgement is seen as the worst of all.”
*   Albert Einstein: “If we trace out what we behold and experience through the language of logic, we are doing science; if we show it in forms whose interrelationships are not accessible to our conscious thought but are instinctively recognized as meaningful, we are doing art. Common to both is the devotion to something beyond the personal, removed from the arbitrary.”
*   “Prayer is not doing, but being.”

I’d recommend reading _[Amazing Grace](https://amzn.to/3AVpmHE)_ to anyone who wants to probe Christian vocabulary a little further in the hands of an unabashed, fearlessly direct, open minded, and remarkably cogent writer.

[![Image 4: Amazing Grace by Kathleen Norris book review](https://pollycastor.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/0.jpg)](https://pollycastor.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/0.jpg)

I agree with this author’s dismay over the colossal amount of baggage spiritual terminology has. This is especially true for me who wasn’t brought up with it, but was even true for this author who strayed and then returned to it. I love how candid she is about her experience and how much room she encourages us all to give these words.

This is not a new book (1999) and I found it last summer when I was doing a book purge of my office. I had not yet read it but liked previous work by this author. So last July, I started reading this a chapter every couple of days, a pace which I felt contributed largely to my enjoyment of the book.

Kathleen Norris is a poet and as such writes incredibly well. She can cut directly and incisively to the heart of something, and she can also take the long way around spiraling in on her point. This journey with her coming back to the Presbyterian church, via needed nourishment from Benedictine nuns, is soul expanding to read.

Each chapter tackles a word used in faith circles, like redemption, sin, prayer, antichrist, grace, unchurched, chosen, theology, asceticism, pentecostal, trinity, mystic, creeds, blood, repentance, righteousness, annunciation, salvation, detachment, belief, doubt, intolerance, worship, hell, apocalypse, and many more.

Not surprisingly, I loved some chapters, and others did not care that much about. Because of this, it probably reflects more of my unevenness than the author’s, that I give this book four stars. It would be great to read together with a group to discuss the ideas further, and our book group has slated it for February to do just that.

Here are the bits that stood out to me, although these quotes lose a bit of their punch out of context:

*   “To say ‘yes’ is to make a leap of faith, to risk oneself in a new and often scary relationship.”
*   “I was startled by the words that had come flying out of my mouth; as so often happens when I am put on the spot, I had said things I hadn’t fully realized were true until I’d said them.”
*   “Our words are wiser than we are.”
*   “What the pastor said was so simple that it will remain with me forever. ‘Each of us acts as the anti-Christ,’ he said, ‘whenever we hear the gospel and do not do it.”
*   Silence liberates the imagination. “Silence reminds me to take my soul with me wherever I go.”
*   “The Hebrew word for salvation means literally ‘to make wide,’ or to ‘make sufficient.'”
*   “Paul makes it clear that if we take inordinate pride in the spiritual gifts we have been blessed with, the joke is on us.”
*   “One sixth-century monk, Dorotheus of Gaza, describes detachment as being free from wanting certain things to happen, and remaining so trusting of God that what is happening will be the thing you want and you will be at peace with all.”
*   “Conversion is a process; it is not a goal, not a product we consume… Conversion is no more spectacular than learning to love the people we live with and work among. Conversion is seeing ourselves, and the ordinary people in our families, our classrooms, and on the job in a new light.”
*   “Addictions and their aftermath take people to the depths of evil…Admitting to addiction often makes people humble, less willing to trust in their self-will alone. And that, the desert monks would say, is half the battle.”
*   “Who has not felt the sudden lifting of what had seemed an unbearable burden, the removal of what for too long had been an insurmountable obstacle? Who does not have something deep within that they would not wish to exorcise, so that it no longer casts a shadow on their capacity to receive and give love?”
*   “Perfectionism is one of the scariest words I know… The word that has been translated as ‘perfect’ does not mean to set forth an impossible goal, or the perfectionism that would have me strive for it at any cost. It is taken from a Latin word meaning complete, entire, full-grown. To those who originally heard it, the word would convey ‘mature’ rather than what we mean today by ‘perfect… Maturity for one person is different from maturity for another… This sort of perfection demands that we become fully ourselves as God would have us: mature, ripe, full, ready for what befalls us, for whatever is to come.'”
*   “Receive a guest with the same attitude you have when you are alone; when alone; maintain alone the same attitude you have in receiving guests.”
*   “Prayer is not asking for what you think you want but asking to be changed in ways you can’t imagine.”
*   “At its Greek root, ‘to believe’ simply means ‘to give one’s heart to.’ Thus, if we can determine what it is we give our heart to, then we will know what it is we believe.”
*   “I had thought my doubts were spectacular obstacles to my faith and was confused but intrigued when an old monk blithely stated that doubt is merely the seed of faith, a sign that faith is alive and ready to grow.”
*   “It took me a long time to recognize that the desire to worship is in itself a significant form of belief.”
*   “ambivalence is a sacred emotion.”
*   “When the mystery of God’s love breaks through into my consciousness, do I run from it?… Or am I virgin enough to respond from my deepest, truest self, and say something new, a ‘yes’ that will change me forever?”
*   Jung knew that what we reject as ‘nothing’ always gets us in the end.”
*   “Idolatry makes love impossible.”
*   “Unfortunately it is scorn for others that often marks religion’s public face in America.”
*   “Righteous: at its root in Hebrew, the words means ‘one whose aim is true,'”
*   “Hope may be a kind of name for God.”
*   “God is identified through relationship. One that demands great willingness to trust and to take risks.”
*   “Thomas Aquinas said that God was active, always in motion– an ocean of being, the sun lighting up the atmosphere; not a noun, but a verb. The-God-Who-Is,’
*   “I have come to think of Mary as the patron saint of ‘both/and’ passion over ‘either/or’ reasoning… as simultaneously Virgin and Mother.”
*   “I wonder if holiness is not the ability to apply one’s anger in quietly working against systemic evil, taking care not to draw undue attention to oneself.”
*   “When it is absolutely necessary to correct another, do so, they said. But do it quickly and simply, then let it go. Don’t get entangled in the expectation of results.”
*   “Much if not most intolerance is at base a stupefying ignorance rather than a deeply rooted conviction.”
*   “Jesus Christ asks us to interpret ourselves, and each other, with the same hospitable, good-hearted diligence that we grant to him. He offers the truth not as a thing but as a way, an opening on the path between the spirit and the letter of the law– a way of forbearance.”
*   “It seems to me that if you can’t ever admit to being a wretch, you haven’t been paying attention.”
*   “Faith is best thought of as a verb, not a ‘thing’ that either you have or you don’t.”
*   “Faith is not synonymous with certainty but is the decision to keep your eyes open.”
*   “Faith then is fragile, something that needs tending.”
*   “Church is about community loving their neighbor as themselves. You go because someone may need you there.”
*   “Worship itself might in fact be a living poem.”
*   “When God-talk is speech that is not of this world, it is a false language.”
*   “Political power seems to corrupt religions, corroding them from within.”
*   “I often think that if I’m a Christian, I’ll be the last to know.”
*   The Rule of St. Benedict states that “all guests who present themselves are to be welcomed as Christ. Benedict knew that hospitality could be life-saving for both monk and guest. He instructs Benedictines not to turn their backs on the world, even as they seek to detach themselves from worldly values. To reject the world is to reject other people, and to reject other people is to reject Christ himself.”
*   “Mary knows that no small part of welcoming a guest is the ability to settle down and listen.”
*   “No woman gives birth to an enemy face.”
*   “The story of Jacob says to me that if we’ve ever truly been forgiven, we have seen the face of God. If we’ve ever been on the receiving end of an act of mercy that made a difference in our lives, we have seen the face of God.”
*   “People who have endured the pain of exile and enslavement are likely to take refuge in the thought that there is punishment for their tormentors, if not in this world then in the next.”
*   “The word ‘apocalypse’ comes from the Greek for ‘uncovering’ or ‘revealing,’ which makes it a word of possibilities.”
*   “When people speak in the same tone of voice about a ‘personal deodorant,’ a ‘personal trainer.’ and a ‘personal Savior,’ I suspect what they really mean is private. (I’ve got mine; too bad about you.) but Christianity, like its ancestor Judaism, is inescapably communal.”
*   “Dogma is not dogmatic dogmatism. The Greek root from which dogma comes means “what seems good, fitting, and becoming.'”
*   “The reality of human sin is admitted, but the sin of casting judgement is seen as the worst of all.”
*   Albert Einstein: “If we trace out what we behold and experience through the language of logic, we are doing science; if we show it in forms whose interrelationships are not accessible to our conscious thought but are instinctively recognized as meaningful, we are doing art. Common to both is the devotion to something beyond the personal, removed from the arbitrary.”
*   “Prayer is not doing, but being.”

I’d recommend reading _[Amazing Grace](https://amzn.to/3AVpmHE)_ to anyone who wants to probe Christian vocabulary a little further in the hands of an unabashed, fearlessly direct, open minded, and remarkably cogent writer.

# Book Club 2014: Amazing Grace (Kozol)

![Image 4](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/15039e540c6936cf54aeff8959034672?s=40&d=%2Fwp-content%2Fthemes%2Ftheblog%2Fimages%2Favatar-2x.jpg&r=G)[Sara-Elizabeth Cottrell](https://musicuentos.com/author/secottrell/)December 12, 2014No Comments
